cf.title: Add amnotifydelete, an index AM callback for deleted tuples

input.subject: Design proposal: grain, exact per-time-bucket aggregates from a summarizing index

verdict_reasoning: The proposal fails at level 1b on already-exists-1 and already-exists-2. It does not say what amnotifydelete does that an AFTER ROW trigger inserting markers cannot, or what core placement adds over an extension beyond the planner path. Demand shown is one workload, and message #1 says TimescaleDB works. Confidence is low because only the author has posted, so the verdict rests on missing answers.

brief.title: Add amnotifydelete index AM callback, first step toward a grain summary index
brief.problem: Index access methods learn of deleted tuples only when VACUUM calls ambulkdelete, so an index that keeps aggregates cannot stay correct within the deleting transaction. The author wants this for time-bucket rollups such as daily count and sum, whose query time grows with rows in the window under btree, BRIN or no index. Materialized views go stale, and trigger-based rollups lock the view on DELETE and UPDATE and fail under REPEATABLE READ.
brief.proposed_design: Patch 1 adds an optional amnotifydelete callback. The executor passes it the recomputed index values of the old tuple version on DELETE, on non-HOT UPDATE, and on matching paths in MERGE, ON CONFLICT, logical replication apply and REPACK (CONCURRENTLY). Later patches add a grain index type that owns hidden summary and marker tables plus a metapage watermark W, a sealer that advances W after WaitForLockers, and a planner path.
user_visible_surface: C API: new amnotifydelete member in IndexAmRoutine, NULL for all existing index AMs.
Planned SQL: create index ... using grain (ts) include (cols) with (buckets = '1 minute, 1 hour, 1 day').
Planned function pg_grain_buckets(index, from, to) to read the summaries.
Planned hidden summary and marker tables owned by the index, visible to pg_dump and pg_upgrade.
Planned planner path for group by date_bin(...) over a grain index.
author_claims: Tables without an opted-in index pay one cached relcache check per row; one-row DELETE and UPDATE timings match master.
DELETE of every row on 1 million rows took about 555 ms with dummy_index_am using the callback, against about 463 ms on master.
On 119M NYC taxi rows, the grain prototype answers daily 30-day queries in 0.134 ms against 896 ms for plain GROUP BY.
Results are exact, including after late writes, because they rely only on locks and MVCC visibility.
The summary table is under 2% of the table size.
brief.thread_state: Only the author has posted: the design, v1 and v2 of patch 1, and prototype numbers for patch 2. No one has replied, and his five design questions are unanswered.
unclear: The write cost of grain on inserts, updates and deletes; the author says he has not measured it.
How the sealer runs every minute: a background worker, cron job or manual call.
Whether WaitForLockers every minute blocks or delays busy write workloads.
How hidden index-owned tables appear in catalogs, pg_dump, pg_upgrade and permissions.
Why patch 1 should go in before anyone has accepted the index type that needs it.

prior_attempts.title: Incremental Materialized View Maintenance
prior_attempts.quote: There has been some feedback sent lately and no update for one month, so I am marking it as RwF for now.
prior_attempts.reason: Michael Paquier marked the entry Returned with Feedback after a month with no update. In July 2022 huyajun had reported bugs: a deadlock between TRUNCATE and concurrent INSERT, wrong counts after concurrent DELETEs, crashes on mismatched column lists, and an unwanted unique index on cross joins. The author said he was still working on them. Paquier also noted little design discussion in three years, and Greg Stark had earlier called the patch hard to review.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P1 kept aggregates current with AFTER triggers on a materialized view. This proposal keeps them in an index-owned summary table, using an executor callback, markers and a sealer watermark, so writers do not lock a shared rollup row.

objections.title: Row-level triggers already deliver old values within the deleting transaction
objections.failure_scenario: A committer accepts amnotifydelete, which runs on every DELETE, non-HOT UPDATE, MERGE, ON CONFLICT, apply and REPACK path. Postgres now has two per-row notifications of deleted tuples, AFTER ROW triggers and this callback, and every future write path must remember to call both. If a new path misses the callback, nothing fails loudly, and a grain index silently drifts from the table.
objections.argument: An AFTER ROW DELETE or UPDATE trigger already receives the old row in the deleting transaction, which is the need the commit message states. Message #1 rejects triggers by pointing to the IVM patch, which locks the view and errors under REPEATABLE READ. But grain's own protocol only inserts marker rows when the time key is before W, and a trigger can do that without locking any summary row. The proposal does not show what the callback can do that such a trigger cannot.
objections.author_must_show: Which step of the grain protocol cannot be done by a C row trigger that inserts markers, with the same WaitForLockers sealer, and why?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 rejects triggers because the IVM patch locks the view and fails under REPEATABLE READ. Inserting a marker row needs neither, and the proposal does not say what the callback does that an always-enabled C row trigger cannot.

objections.title: The rollup can be built as an extension; core placement needs a reason
objections.failure_scenario: The project adds a grain index type with index-owned hidden heaps, new pg_dump and pg_upgrade handling, and a planner path. Every later catalog, dump or upgrade change must then account for a new kind of relation ownership. Users who need rollups today can already use TimescaleDB continuous aggregates, which merge stored buckets with recent raw rows past a watermark.
objections.argument: Message #1 says TimescaleDB works for this and calls it too heavy for one rollup. That makes it a convenience gap, since the job can be done today. A summary table, a marker table, a trigger, a sealer run by a background worker, and a pg_grain_buckets() function all fit in an extension. The thread has no demand beyond the author's own workload and no reply from anyone else.
objections.author_must_show: What does core placement give grain that an extension built on triggers, a background worker and a set-returning function cannot have, apart from the planner path?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 says TimescaleDB works and objects only to its weight, which is a convenience argument. The material does not show what an extension with a trigger, a background worker and a function cannot do, apart from the planner path.

other_surviving.title: Index-owned hidden tables have no defined dump, upgrade or publication behaviour
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A user creates a grain index, then runs pg_upgrade or adds the table to a publication for all tables. pg_upgrade may not carry over the summary and marker tables, or the metapage watermark W may stop matching them. A publication may replicate the hidden tables or skip them, and the user learns which only when counts on the subscriber or the new cluster go wrong.
other_surviving.argument: Message #1 says the hidden tables are ordinary tables owned by the index "the way a TOAST table is owned". TOAST has its own special handling in pg_dump, pg_upgrade, publications, GRANT and \d, and none of that is designed here. Open question 3 in message #1 leaves this unresolved, and message #4 says patch 2 depends on it. Patch 1 is being proposed before the consumer's contract with these tools is settled.
other_surviving.author_must_show: How do pg_dump, pg_upgrade, publications, GRANT and psql \d each treat the summary and marker tables and the watermark W?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 leaves the pg_dump and pg_upgrade handling of the hidden tables open as question 3, and says nothing on publications or privileges. Message #4 says patch 2 depends on that answer, and the answer is missing.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: A never-scanned index breaks what tools expect of an index
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A DBA runs reindexdb --concurrently across a database, and it fails on the grain index because the documented contract has ambuild refuse ii_Concurrent. A monitoring tool sees idx_scan = 0 on the grain index and suggests dropping it, which removes the rollup. Neither user finds out until a script fails or the queries slow down.
other_surviving.argument: Message #1 says "The index is never scanned", and reads go through pg_grain_buckets(). The patch 1 docs tell summarizing indexes to refuse CONCURRENTLY builds, so CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY and REINDEX CONCURRENTLY stop working for this kind of object. Open question 1 asks whether this needs its own DDL. A committer would likely ask why an index object is used when the behaviour is closer to a materialized view.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Which existing index operations (REINDEX CONCURRENTLY, idx_scan statistics, amcheck, pg_repack) would work on a grain index, and why is an index better than new DDL here?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 says the index is never scanned, and the patch 1 docs let ambuild refuse concurrent builds, so `REINDEX CONCURRENTLY` can fail on it. The author's question 1 asks the same thing and nobody has answered it.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Callback enters the extension API before its only consumer's design is accepted
other_surviving.failure_scenario: amnotifydelete ships in version 20 with this signature and call contract. Patch 2 then needs the new tuple version, an abort hook, or a broader amupdate() shape. The project must either change a published IndexAmRoutine member, which breaks out-of-core AMs built against it, or keep a callback no in-core AM uses.
other_surviving.argument: The author's open question 2 in message #1 asks whether a delete callback or a broader amupdate() is right, and nobody has answered it. Message #4 says patch 2's shape depends on whether an index may own tables. The only in-tree user is dummy_index_am. An index AM callback is hard to reshape once extensions use it, so committing patch 1 first fixes the contract before the design that defines it is settled.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Which parts of the grain design, including the hidden tables and the sealer, does the amnotifydelete signature already fully cover, so no later change to it is needed?

critic.reasoning: IndexAmRoutine does change between major versions, so the cost to out-of-core AMs is smaller than stated. But the author's own question 2 (delete callback or amupdate) is unanswered, and dummy_index_am is the only user.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Grain summaries can expose rows hidden by row-level security or column privileges
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A multi-tenant orders table uses RLS so each tenant sees only its own rows. A tenant role calls pg_grain_buckets on the grain index, or runs a group by date_bin query that the planned path answers from the summary table. It gets count and sum over every tenant's rows, and nothing in any log shows this.
other_surviving.argument: The summary table holds count, sum, min and max over all rows that match the index predicate, computed by the sealer under one snapshot with no RLS policy or role applied (message #1). The proposal does not say which privileges pg_grain_buckets checks, whether the summary is skipped when RLS is active or when the caller lacks SELECT on the INCLUDE columns, or who may read the hidden tables. Message #1 question 3 asks only about namespace and pg_dump, so the privilege model is still open. Patch 1 itself has no privilege aspect.
other_surviving.author_must_show: When a table has RLS policies or column privileges on INCLUDE columns, how do pg_grain_buckets and the planner path avoid returning aggregates over rows or columns the caller cannot select?

critic.reasoning: The sealer computes summaries over all rows that match the index predicate, and the material names no privilege or RLS check for pg_grain_buckets or the planner path. The multi-tenant scenario is concrete and nothing in the thread answers it.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Every future tuple-removing path must call amnotifydelete, with no loud failure
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A later release adds a new path that deletes or replaces heap tuples, such as a new MERGE action or another repack mode, and does not call amnotifydelete. Every existing test passes, because no in-core index uses the callback. Users of a summarizing index get wrong counts and find out only when they compare against the base table.
other_surviving.argument: The documentation hunk lists seven call sites: DELETE, non-HOT UPDATE, MERGE delete, partition move, logical apply, REPACK (CONCURRENTLY) replay and ON CONFLICT speculative removal. The summary stays exact only if that list stays complete forever. No in-core AM sets the callback, so only dummy_index_am tests would notice a missing call. The HOT rules for summarizing indexes are subtle: [P21] reverted a BRIN HOT change because visibility info did not keep summaries correct.
other_surviving.author_must_show: What check or test would fail if a future executor or table AM path removes a tuple without calling amnotifydelete?

precedents.title: Revert changes in HOT handling of BRIN indexes

critic.reasoning: No in-core AM sets the callback, so only dummy_index_am tests would catch a new path that skips it. [P21] is about HOT and BRIN summaries, not about missed call sites, and must not be used as support.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

refuted.title: Metapage watermark and hidden summary tables have no pg_upgrade pairing rule
refuted.failure_scenario: A user runs pg_upgrade on a cluster with a grain index. The index file, which holds W, is transferred, but binary-upgrade dump recreates the summary or marker tables with new relfilenumbers or empty contents. W then no longer matches the summary rows, and pg_grain_buckets returns stale or wrong totals with no error.
refuted.argument: Exactness in message #1 rests on W in the index metapage and the hidden summary and marker tables staying consistent. The proposal leaves open how pg_dump and pg_upgrade handle index-owned heaps (open question 3) and how the metapage is WAL-logged (open question 5). TOAST has dedicated binary-upgrade handling for this kind of ownership, and a new owner relation needs the same, plus rules for REINDEX and DROP.
refuted.author_must_show: How do pg_dump --binary-upgrade and pg_upgrade keep W and the hidden summary and marker tables consistent, and what do REINDEX and DROP INDEX do to those tables?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1, whose failure scenario already covers W no longer matching the hidden tables after pg_upgrade.

refuted.title: Patch 1 adds a core API whose only planned user is unaccepted
refuted.failure_scenario: The callback is committed and becomes part of IndexAmRoutine. The grain design then changes, for example to its own DDL or to a broader amupdate(), and the callback no longer fits. Core keeps an API with no in-core caller, and extension AMs that adopted it block later changes to it.
refuted.argument: Message #1 asks for a blessing of the callback before the index type exists. The author's own questions 1 and 2 ask whether an index is the right object and whether a delete callback or amupdate() is right. Both answers decide the callback's shape. In message #4 the author says patch 2 depends on those answers. Committing patch 1 first fixes the API before its consumer's design is settled. No one has replied in the thread, so no committer has taken on this area.
refuted.author_must_show: Which in-core or extension index AM other than grain would use amnotifydelete in its current form, and would grain's answers to questions 1 and 2 change it?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of replication-ondisk-1. The added remark that no committer has replied is a committability point and does not strengthen the design objection.

refuted.title: Index-owned hidden heaps add a new relation kind to many subsystems
refuted.failure_scenario: An index owns a summary table and a marker table. pg_dump, pg_upgrade, REINDEX, ALTER INDEX SET TABLESPACE, DROP and the privilege checks each need rules for them. Any command that misses one leaves orphaned tables, or loses the summaries after an upgrade. The DBA finds out at upgrade or restore time.
refuted.argument: Message #1 compares the hidden tables to TOAST. TOAST is owned by a table, and its special cases are spread across the tree after many years. An index that owns heaps is a new dependency kind, and every later command that handles indexes must account for it. The author leaves the namespace and the pg_dump and pg_upgrade handling open as question 3, so this cost is not yet weighed against the use case.
refuted.author_must_show: Which existing commands that handle indexes need changes for index-owned tables, and could the summaries live in a mechanism that already has pg_dump and pg_upgrade support?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1: both ask how existing commands and tools treat index-owned tables, which is the author's open question 3.

refuted.title: Patch 1 adds an executor-wide hook with no accepted consumer
refuted.failure_scenario: amnotifydelete is committed for version 20, but the grain index type is never accepted. Every later change to DELETE, UPDATE, MERGE, ON CONFLICT, apply or REPACK must keep calling the hook correctly. Only dummy_index_am exercises it, so a missed call goes unnoticed until an out-of-core AM silently returns wrong aggregates.
refuted.argument: Message #1 asks for a blessing on the callback before the index type exists. Message #4 says the shape of patch 2 depends on two unanswered questions: whether an index is the right object, and whether an index may own tables. If either answer is no, the hook has no user. Every table pays a per-row relcache check, and every executor author keeps the call sites correct, for a benefit that may never ship.
refuted.author_must_show: Will you hold patch 1 until the grain design is accepted, or name a second index AM, in core or out of tree, that would use amnotifydelete?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of replication-ondisk-1 and maintenance-fit-1. Its one separate point, the per-row relcache check, is answered by message #1, where one-row DELETE and UPDATE timings match master.

refuted.title: Demand shown is one workload, not yet independent users
refuted.failure_scenario: The project builds an index type with index-owned hidden tables, a sealer and a planner path. The users who need exact time-bucket rollups already run TimescaleDB or an extension. The new pieces then serve few users while the catalog, pg_dump and pg_upgrade work stays with the project.
refuted.argument: The only demand in the material is the author's own orders query and the taxi benchmark in messages #1 and #4. Nobody else posted in the thread. The IVM patch [P1] and TimescaleDB show that rollups are wanted in general. They do not show that this narrow form is wanted in core: one timestamptz key, integer columns, fixed bucket widths. Message #1 calls TimescaleDB a working solution, and the objection to it is that it is too heavy.
refuted.author_must_show: Which users besides your own workload need exact per-bucket aggregates in core, and why do the existing extensions not meet their needs?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of already-exists-2, which already states that the thread shows no demand beyond the author's workload and that TimescaleDB does the job.

touch_points.label: on-disk format / pg_upgrade
touch_points.reason: The planned grain index keeps watermark W in its metapage and owns hidden summary and marker tables that pg_upgrade must carry over.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: Patch 1 adds calls in the logical replication apply paths; question 5 leaves the metapage WAL logging open.

touch_points.label: catalog changes
touch_points.reason: The planned index-owned hidden tables are a new kind of relation ownership; patch 1 adds a relcache flag.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: Patch 1 adds the amnotifydelete member to IndexAmRoutine.

touch_points.label: SQL-standard conflict or non-standard syntax
touch_points.reason: Planned `create index ... using grain ... with (buckets = ...)` and pg_grain_buckets() add non-standard surface.

touch_points.label: planner behaviour change
touch_points.reason: Patch 3 plans a planner path for group by date_bin(...) over a grain index.

touch_points.label: pg_dump / restore round-trip
touch_points.reason: Question 3 in message #1 leaves open how pg_dump handles the hidden summary and marker tables.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: The summaries aggregate all rows matching the index predicate, with no stated RLS or column privilege check on reads.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: Every current and future tuple-removing path must call amnotifydelete, and only dummy_index_am tests it.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: Every DELETE and non-HOT UPDATE on every table pays one cached relcache check per row.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: Message #1 says TimescaleDB works, and the protocol may fit in an extension built on triggers.

questions: Which step of the grain protocol cannot be done by a C row trigger that inserts markers, with the same WaitForLockers sealer?
What does core placement give grain that an extension with triggers, a background worker and a set-returning function cannot have, apart from the planner path?
Would the answers to your questions 1 and 2 change the amnotifydelete signature or call contract, and if so, why should patch 1 go in first?
What is the write cost of a grain index on inserts, updates and deletes, including marker inserts for rows before W?
How does the sealer run every minute, and how long does its WaitForLockers call wait when a long write transaction is open?

committability.owner_note: It needs a committer who knows the index AM API and the executor's ModifyTable and logical apply paths. Nobody but the author has posted.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a permanent IndexAmRoutine member and for every tuple-removing path calling it correctly. A missed call gives wrong aggregates with no error.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted v1 two days after the design and a rebased v2 with a CI fix eight days later, which suggests he stays engaged.

priority.reason: The thread shows one workload and no replies, so the audience is not shown. The patch is about 51 KiB across the executor, relcache, repack and logical apply, and its only planned user still has five open design questions.

provisional_note: Without the code, nobody can check whether patch 1 covers every tuple-removing path or what the relcache check costs under concurrency. Message #4 was not shown, and the grain index type is not written.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Incremental Materialized View Maintenance
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add incremental materialized views (CREATE INCREMENTAL MATERIALIZED VIEW) that Postgres keeps current in the same transaction as base table changes, using AFTER triggers and transition tables. The patch computes deltas from the view definition and applies them to the view, with support for joins, some built-in aggregates, EXISTS subqueries and outer joins.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier marked the entry Returned with Feedback after a month with no update. In July 2022 huyajun had reported bugs: a deadlock between TRUNCATE and concurrent INSERT, wrong counts after concurrent DELETEs, crashes on mismatched column lists, and an unwanted unique index on cross joins. The author said he was still working on them. Paquier also noted little design discussion in three years, and Greg Stark had earlier called the patch hard to review.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
There has been some feedback sent lately and no update
for one month, so I am marking it as RwF for now.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add callback table access method to reset filenode when dropping relation
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a relation_reset_filenode callback to the table access method interface, called from heap_drop_with_catalog when a table is dropped, as the counterpart of relation_set_new_filenode. The goal was to let table AMs with non-file storage, such as an in-memory table, clean up their storage on DROP TABLE.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund and Heikki Linnakangas pointed out that dropping storage must happen at commit or abort and be redone from the commit record during WAL replay, which cannot run AM-specific code. A callback at drop time, or xact callbacks run at commit, therefore cannot drop storage correctly. Heikki suggested using smgrGetPendingDeletes() instead. The patch then stopped applying, the author did not reply when asked whether he was waiting for feedback, and the entry was marked Returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I don't think implementing dropping relation data at-commit/rollback using
xact callbacks can be correct. The dropping needs to be integrated with the
commit / abort records, so it is redone during crash recovery - that's not
possible with xact callbacks.

precedents_retrieved.title: Inconsistency in owner assignment between INDEX and STATISTICS
precedents_retrieved.summary: The proposal makes CREATE STATISTICS record the table owner as the owner of the statistics object, as CREATE INDEX does, in place of the user who runs the command. The patch sets stxowner from the relation's relowner in CreateStatistics() and keeps the permission check on the current user.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Amit Khandekar pointed out that the documentation states statistics ownership is independent of the underlying table, so the creator owning the object is intended. He also showed that the reproduction was wrong: the statistics object was created in the default schema, and dropping it there gives the expected "must be owner" error. The author agreed with both points and withdrew the proposal.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I think, since there is no permanent association of ownership between
the table and the statistics, it makes sense for the user who is
running the create command to own the statistics, regardless of who
the user is, provided that the user has privileges.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Show index search count in EXPLAIN ANALYZE."
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Show index search count in EXPLAIN ANALYZE."
Reverted commit(s): Show index search count in EXPLAIN ANALYZE.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 5ead85fbc81162ab1594f656b036a22e814f96b3.

This commit shows test failures with debug_parallel_query=regress.  The

precedents_retrieved.title: DELETE CASCADE
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a `DELETE CASCADE` statement that treats existing NO ACTION and RESTRICT foreign keys as CASCADE for that one statement. The goal is to delete rows with dependents without redefining the constraints.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch stopped applying, and the author did not reply for about four months, so Julien Rouhaud closed it under the commitfest rules. The design was still open. David G. Johnston preferred making FK actions changeable with ALTER CONSTRAINT, and Tom Lane suggested `SET CONSTRAINTS ... ON DELETE referential_action`, which names the constraints explicitly. Julien said the feature itself is wanted and a resubmission is expected.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: It's been almost 4 months since your last email, and almost 2 weeks since the notice that this patch doesn't apply anymore.

precedents_retrieved.title: Free memory allocated by waitonlock_error_callback()
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a pfree() in waitonlock_error_callback() for the StringInfo buffer it allocates in ErrorContext. The goal was to stop Valgrind from reporting the memory as definitely lost.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that commit 89d57c1fb had already solved this leak in a more general way. The author confirmed that 89d57c1fb fixed the reported issue and withdrew the patch. Michael Paquier had also noted that errfinish() resets ErrorContext, so the leak was not real.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Didn't 89d57c1fb already solve this in a more
general way?

precedents_retrieved.title: Remove page-read callback from XLogReaderState
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch removes the page-read callback (and later the open and close segment callbacks) from XLogReaderState. XLogReadRecord becomes a state machine that returns XLREAD_NEED_DATA, and the caller then loads WAL pages itself.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Thomas Munro committed a squashed version in April 2021, and it was later reverted. The author's note mentions a possible defect on one platform but does not give the cause. In September 2021 Thomas Munro pointed the author to a message from Andres Freund that the author had not seen and had not yet answered, and the entry was then returned with feedback. The visible messages do not show the content of that message or the exact reason for the revert.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add statistics refresh materialized view
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add per-view statistics for REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW (execution count and last refresh time) to the statistics collector, exposed as new columns in pg_stat_all_tables and its user/sys variants. The aim was to record when and how often each materialized view was refreshed without relying on pg_stat_statements.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Fujii Masao objected that adding columns to pg_stat_all_tables for one utility command is a poor design: it singles out REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW over commands such as TRUNCATE or CLUSTER, would lead to many per-command columns, and the columns would be useless for most entries, which are tables. He also suggested that pg_stat_statements and log_statement could already provide the information per view. The author agreed that these tools may be sufficient for most use cases and withdrew the proposal, and the entry was marked Returned with Feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
It's not good design to add new columns per utility command into
pg_stat_all_tables. Otherwise pg_stat_all_tables will have to have lots of
columns to expose the stats of many utility commands at last.

precedents_retrieved.title: Lock updated tuples in tuple_update() and tuple_delete()
precedents_retrieved.summary: When tuple_update() or tuple_delete() finds a concurrently updated tuple in read committed mode, the table AM locks the updated version itself instead of returning TM_Updated for a separate tuple_lock() call. Later versions also had update and delete return the old tuple through a slot passed by the executor, which avoids refetching it and helps table AMs with costly TID lookups.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Version 15 was committed in March 2023, then reverted after Andres Freund's post-commit review. He showed that RETURNING could use the wrong tuple, with an isolation test that fails. He also criticised the new API: the ignored wait parameter, tmfd turned into an input, and the LazyTupleTableSlot code. The redesigned old-tuple API came days before the version 16 feature freeze, and he said it was not ready for 16. In March 2024 the author planned to push a revised version, and the visible messages do not show why the entry was finally returned with feedback in October 2024.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I guess this really is part of my issue with this change - it optimizes the rare case, while not addressing the same inefficiency in the common case.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Refactor CopyReadAttributes{CSV,Text}() to use a callback in COPY FROM"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Refactor CopyReadAttributes{CSV,Text}() to use a callback in COPY FROM"
Reverted commit(s): Refactor CopyReadAttributes{CSV,Text}() to use a callback in COPY FROM; Revert "Refactor CopyAttributeOut{CSV,Text}() to use a callback in COPY TO"
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 95fb5b49024, for reasons similar to what led to
1aa8324b81fa.  In this case, the callback was called once per row, which
is less worse than the previous callback introduced for COPY TO called
once per argument for each row, still the patch set discussed to plug in
custom routines to the COPY paths would be able to know which subroutine
to use depending on its CopyFromState, so this led to a suboptimal
approach at the end.

For now, this part is reverted to consider better which approach to use.

precedents_retrieved.title: Improve management of SLRU statistics collection.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Improve management of SLRU statistics collection.
Reverted commit(s): Move each SLRU's lwlocks to a separate tranche.; Collect statistics about SLRU caches
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Instead of re-identifying which statistics bucket to use for a given
SLRU on every counter increment, do it once during shmem initialization.
This saves a fair number of cycles, and there's no real cost because
we could not have a bucket assignment that varies over time or across
backends anyway.

Also, get rid of the ill-considered decision to let pgstat.c pry
directly into SLRU's shared state; it's cleaner just to have slru.c
pass the stats bucket number.

In consequence of these changes, there's no longer any need to store
an SLRU's LWLock tranche info in shared memory, so get rid of that,
making this a net reduction in shmem consumption.  (That partly
reverts fe702a7b3.)

This is basically code review for 28cac71bd, so I also cleaned up
some comments, removed a dangling extern declaration, fixed some
things that should be static and/or const, etc.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert changes in HOT handling of BRIN indexes
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert changes in HOT handling of BRIN indexes
Reverted commit(s): Ignore BRIN indexes when checking for HOT udpates; Move test for BRIN HOT behavior to stats.sql
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commits 5753d4ee32 and fe60b67250 that modified HOT to
ignore BRIN indexes. The commit message for 5753d4ee32 claims that:

    When determining whether an index update may be skipped by using
    HOT, we can ignore attributes indexed only by BRIN indexes. There
    are no index pointers to individual tuples in BRIN, and the page
    range summary will be updated anyway as it relies on visibility
    info.

This is partially incorrect - it's true BRIN indexes don't point to
individual tuples, so HOT chains are not an issue, but the visibitlity
info is not sufficient to keep the index up to date. This can easily
result in corrupted indexes, as demonstrated in the hackers thread.

This does not mean relaxing the HOT restrictions for BRIN is a lost
cause, but it needs to handle the two aspects (allowing HOT chains and
updating the page range summaries) as separate. But that requires a
major changes, and it's too late for that in the current dev cycle.

roaster_notes.note: Only P1 is a close relative, and its recorded reason was inactivity, which does not apply here. Its summary also reports wrong counts after concurrent deletes, but that is an AI summary and does not support an objection on its own. Message #1 cites amtargetdelete and amupdate as earlier callback proposals but does not say why they were not accepted, and the material does not record it either. So no earlier rejection reason can be checked against this design. P21 (BRIN HOT revert) is in the same area, but this patch notifies summarizing indexes on updates that add entries, so the visibility-only gap behind that revert does not apply.
Patch 1 alone adds a C callback that is NULL for existing AMs and changes no SQL, dump or client-visible behaviour. Both objections concern the planned surface that the callback is meant to serve.
Patch 1 alone changes no on-disk format, WAL record or wire message. The nbtree VACUUM invariant does not apply, because nbtree only sets the new member to NULL.
Patch 1, the amnotifydelete callback, is a C-level index AM hook with no privilege or exposure aspect. The only objection is about the planned grain index and its read paths.

The nbtree invariant does not apply: the patch only adds a NULL callback entry in nbtree.c and does not change VACUUM behaviour. Hot-path cost for non-users looks small in the shown numbers, so no objection is raised on that.
Two objections raised. Both rest on existing mechanisms, row triggers and an external extension, that appear to cover the need with more effort.
Two demand objections raised. Both are 'not now, show demand', not a rejection of the idea.
